definition: A diagnostic framework that decomposes Return on Equity (ROE) into five distinct operating, financing, and tax components: Tax Burden, Interest Burden, EBIT Margin, Total Asset Turnover, and Financial Leverage.
formula: \text{ROE} = \underbrace{\frac{\text{Net Income}}{\text{EBT}}}_{\text{Tax Burden}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\text{EBT}}{\text{EBIT}}}_{\text{Interest Burden}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\text{EBIT}}{\text{Revenue}}}_{\text{EBIT Margin}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\text{Revenue}}{\text{Avg. Assets}}}_{\text{Asset Turnover}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\text{Avg. Assets}}{\text{Avg. Equity}}}_{\text{Leverage}}
practicalUses: Isolates whether an increase in ROE is driven by genuine operating efficiency or dangerous debt-fueled leverage.
Quantifies the exact drag of rising corporate tax rates or higher refinancing costs on shareholder value creation.
Benchmarking peer firms to identify which factor explains superior capital productivity.
commonPitfalls: Confusing Tax Burden with the Effective Tax Rate: Tax Burden equals 1 - t; higher Tax Burden means a lower tax rate.
Failing to use Average Total Assets and Average Equity when matching flow income-statement items to stock balance-sheet items.
Confusing Interest Burden (EBT / EBIT) with Interest Coverage (EBIT / Interest Expense).

workedNumerical.title: Industrial Peer 5-Way ROE Decomposition
steps: Step 1 (Tax Burden) = Net Income / EBT = 45M / 60M = 0.7500 (Effective tax rate = 25.0%).
Step 5 (Financial Leverage) = Avg. Assets / Avg. Equity = 400M / 200M = 2.0000x.

term: Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF)
regexPattern: \b(Free Cash Flow to the Firm|FCFF|Unlevered Free Cash Flow)\b
definition: The discretionary cash flow generated by core business operations that is available to all providers of capital (debt holders, preferred shareholders, and common equity holders) after fulfilling all reinvestment needs in working capital and fixed capital.
practicalUses: Primary input for DCF enterprise valuation when capital structure is changing or debt levels are non-constant.
Eliminates capital structure bias when comparing cash generation across heavily levered vs unlevered peers.
Measures organic solvency and corporate debt service capacity before financial engineering.
commonPitfalls: Under US GAAP, Interest Expense is included in CFO, so it must be added back after-tax; under IFRS, if interest is classified under Financing activities, no adjustment is made to CFO.
Omitting the tax shield (1 - t) on interest expense add-backs.
Failing to exclude gain on disposal of equipment from Net Income when deriving FCFF from bottom-up.

workedNumerical.title: Deriving FCFF from Cash Flow from Operations (CFO)
given: Cash Flow from Operations (CFO under US GAAP) = 140M USD
Capital Expenditures (Gross Fixed Capital Investment) = 65M USD
Proceeds from Sale of Old Machine = 10M USD
steps: Step 1 (Net FCInv) = Gross CapEx - Disposal Proceeds = 65M - 10M = 55M USD.
Step 2 (After-tax Interest Add-back) = Interest × (1 - t) = 25M × (1 - 0.24) = 19M USD.
Step 3 (FCFF Calculation) = CFO + Interest(1 - t) - Net FCInv = 140M + 19M - 55M = 104M USD.

definition: The cumulative difference between ending inventory reported under the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) method and the First-In, First-Out (FIFO) method. Required under US GAAP footnote disclosures to enable economic comparison with IFRS firms (where LIFO is prohibited).
formula: \begin{aligned} \text{Inventory}_{\text{FIFO}} &= \text{Inventory}_{\text{LIFO}} + \text{LIFO Reserve} \\ \text{COGS}_{\text{FIFO}} &= \text{COGS}_{\text{LIFO}} - \Delta \text{LIFO Reserve} \\ \text{Retained Earnings}_{\text{FIFO}} &= \text{Retained Earnings}_{\text{LIFO}} + \text{LIFO Reserve} \times (1 - t) \end{aligned}
practicalUses: Converts US GAAP inventory figures to economic replacement cost (FIFO) for balance sheet accuracy.
Adjusts Cost of Goods Sold to reflect current inventory purchasing costs vs historical inventory layers.
Critical adjustment in multinational comparative analysis between US GAAP and IFRS competitors.
commonPitfalls: Subtracting ΔLIFO Reserve from LIFO inventory instead of adding it.
LIFO Liquidation trap: when inventory units decline during inflation, old low-cost layers enter COGS, artificially inflating gross margin and tax liabilities.
Forgetting to multiply the cumulative reserve by (1 - t) when calculating the equity / retained earnings adjustment.

workedNumerical.title: Converting Inventory and COGS from LIFO to FIFO
given: Reported LIFO Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) = 890M USD
steps: Step 1 (FIFO Ending Inventory) = LIFO Inventory + Ending LIFO Reserve = 420M + 75M = 495M USD.
Step 2 (Change in LIFO Reserve) = 75M - 50M = 25M USD increase.
Step 3 (FIFO COGS) = LIFO COGS - ΔLIFO Reserve = 890M - 25M = 865M USD.
Step 4 (Pre-tax Cumulative Profit Adjustment) = Ending LIFO Reserve = 75M USD.
workedNumerical.result: FIFO Inventory = 495.00M USD | FIFO COGS = 865.00M USD

regexPattern: \b(Diluted Earnings Per Share|Diluted EPS|If-Converted Method|Treasury Stock Method)\b
definition: A performance metric that measures earnings per share assuming all potentially dilutive convertible bonds, convertible preferred stocks, employee stock options, and warrants are exercised or converted into common stock at the beginning of the period.
formula: \text{Diluted EPS} = \frac{\text{Net Income} - \text{Pref Div} + \text{Conv Debt Interest}(1 - t) + \text{Conv Pref Div}}{\text{Weighted Avg Shares} + \Delta \text{Shares}_{\text{Options}} + \Delta \text{Shares}_{\text{Conv}}}
practicalUses: Protects common equity holders by measuring worst-case per-share cash flow dilution.
Enforces strict anti-dilution filtering: instruments that increase EPS if converted must be excluded.
Standard metric utilized in P/E valuation multiples to avoid inflating valuation through unexercised options.
commonPitfalls: Including anti-dilutive securities in the denominator (if incremental EPS > Basic EPS, do not convert).
Failing to add back after-tax interest savings on convertible debt: add Interest × (1 - t), not gross interest.
Treasury Stock Method mistake: failing to reduce incremental shares by the number of shares bought back using option proceeds at the average market price.

workedNumerical.title: Convertible Bond If-Converted Diluted EPS Test
given: Weighted Average Common Shares Outstanding = 1,000,000 shares
Convertible 6% Bonds = 10,000,000 USD par, convertible into 250,000 common shares
steps: Step 3 (Incremental EPS of Convertible Bond) = 450,000 / 250,000 = 1.80 USD/share.
Step 4 (Anti-dilution Test) = 1.80 < 3.00, therefore the bond IS DILUTIVE and must be included.

regexPattern: \b(Interest Coverage Ratio|Interest Coverage|Times Interest Earned|TIE Ratio)\b
definition: A solvency metric measuring the margin of safety a company has to service interest payments from core operating earnings. Under rigorous CFA analysis, capitalized interest must be added back to interest expense and depreciation of prior capitalized interest must be adjusted in EBIT.
formula: \text{Adjusted Interest Coverage} = \frac{\text{EBIT} + \text{Depr of Capitalized Interest}}{\text{Gross Interest Expense} + \text{Capitalized Interest}}
practicalUses: Evaluates corporate creditworthiness and probability of debt covenant breach.
Uncovers aggressive accounting where companies capitalize interest into PPE to hide debt costs from the income statement.
Primary quantitative input in credit rating agency models (Moody's, S&P) for investment grade vs high yield rating.
commonPitfalls: Using Net Interest Expense instead of Gross Interest (interest income is non-operating and can vanish during liquidity stress).
Ignoring capitalized interest, which understates true interest obligations and overstates coverage.
Comparing EBITDA coverage directly to EBIT coverage without accounting for maintenance CapEx.

workedNumerical.title: Adjusting Interest Coverage for Construction Capitalized Interest
given: Reported Income Statement Interest Expense = 20M USD
Capitalized Interest in PPE for Current Year = 10M USD
Depreciation of Prior Years' Capitalized Interest included in COGS = 3M USD
steps: Step 1 (Adjusted EBIT) = Reported EBIT + Prior Cap. Interest Depr = 95M + 3M = 98M USD.
Step 2 (Total Gross Interest Incurred) = Reported Interest + Current Capitalized Interest = 20M + 10M = 30M USD.

definition: Balance sheet items resulting from temporary timing differences between the accounting carrying value of an asset or liability and its tax base. DTLs reflect future tax cash outflows; DTAs reflect future tax deductions or credits.
formula: \begin{aligned} \text{DTL / DTA}_{\text{Asset}} &= (\text{Carrying Value} - \text{Tax Base}) \times t_{\text{enacted}} \\ \text{Income Tax Expense} &= \text{Taxes Payable} + \Delta \text{DTL} - \Delta \text{DTA} \end{aligned}
practicalUses: Determines whether an enacted statutory corporate tax rate change causes a non-cash gain or loss on revaluation.
Adjusts balance sheet leverage: DTLs not expected to reverse (e.g. growing capital expenditure base) are reclassified as equity.
Assesses earnings quality: an increase in valuation allowance against DTAs indicates declining management confidence in future profitability.
commonPitfalls: Reversing the rules: For Assets, Carrying Value > Tax Base produces a DTL; for Liabilities, Carrying Value > Tax Base produces a DTA.
Treating permanent differences (e.g. tax-free municipal interest, regulatory fines) as deferred taxes (they never create DTL/DTA).
Failing to remeasure all existing DTL and DTA balances immediately when new future tax legislation is officially enacted.

workedNumerical.title: Impact of Enacted Tax Rate Reduction on DTL and Tax Expense
given: Equipment Cost = 600,000 USD (Straight-line 3 years book; MACRS 50%/50% for tax)
Year 1 End Carrying Value = 400,000 USD; Tax Base = 300,000 USD
Tax rate changes from 30% to newly enacted 25% for subsequent years
steps: Step 1 (Temporary Difference) = Carrying Value - Tax Base = 400,000 - 300,000 = 100,000 USD (DTL).
Step 2 (Remeasured Ending DTL) = 100,000 × 25% = 25,000 USD (at 30% it would have been 30,000 USD).
Step 4 (Income Tax Expense) = Taxes Payable + ΔDTL = 85,000 + 25,000 = 110,000 USD.
workedNumerical.result: Ending DTL = 25,000 USD | Income Tax Expense = 110,000 USD

definition: An 8-variable quantitative probit model designed to detect earnings manipulation and financial statement fraud before it is revealed by auditor restatement or regulatory enforcement. An M-Score greater than -1.78 indicates high probability of manipulation.
practicalUses: Identifies channel stuffing via disproportionate Days Sales in Receivables Index (DSRI > 1.0).
Catches aggressive capitalisation of operating expenses via the Asset Quality Index (AQI > 1.0).
Forensic accounting screen applied to short equity ideas and forensic portfolio risk controls.
commonPitfalls: Negative number comparison error: -1.45 is GREATER than -1.78 (closer to zero), so -1.45 indicates high probability of manipulation, whereas -2.20 indicates non-manipulation.
Misinterpreting DEPI (Depreciation Index): DEPI > 1.0 means depreciation rate decreased, signalling extended asset lives to boost earnings.
Overlooking that SGAI and LEVI have negative coefficients in the standard 8-factor specification.

workedNumerical.title: Evaluating Manipulation Probability Against the -1.78 Cutoff
given: Composite weighted contribution of DSRI, GMI, AQI, SGI, DEPI, SGAI, LEVI = +2.65
Net Income = 90M USD; Operating Cash Flow (CFO) = 40M USD
steps: Step 1 (Accruals Ratio) = (Net Income - CFO) / Total Assets = (90M - 40M) / 500M = 0.1000.
Step 4 (Assessment) = Since -1.7221 > -1.78, company is classified as a PROBABLE EARNINGS MANIPULATOR.

regexPattern: \b(Total Periodic Pension Cost|TPPC|Periodic Pension Cost|Funded Status)\b
definition: The true economic cost incurred by a company to maintain its defined-benefit pension obligation over the reporting period, reflecting changes in the net balance sheet funded status adjusted for employer cash contributions.
formula: \begin{aligned} \text{Funded Status} &= \text{Fair Value of Plan Assets} - \text{PBO} \\ \text{TPPC} &= \text{Contributions} - (\text{Ending Funded Status} - \text{Beginning Funded Status}) \\ &= \text{Current Service} + \text{Past Service} + \text{Interest Cost} - \text{Actual Return on Assets} \pm \text{Actuarial Losses} \end{aligned}
practicalUses: Eliminates accounting smoothing permitted under US GAAP / IFRS to reveal the true economic cash drain of pension deficits.
Classifies operating vs financing pension components: only Current Service Cost is core operating expense; interest cost and return on assets belong in financing.
Normalizes EBITDA when comparing companies with defined-benefit vs defined-contribution plans.
commonPitfalls: Confusing Total Periodic Pension Cost (economic) with Reported Pension Cost in P&L (which smooths actuarial gains and uses expected rather than actual asset returns).
Treating Plan Assets and PBO separately rather than as a single net balance sheet liability / asset.
Failing to add back past service cost when amortized over future employee working lives under US GAAP.

workedNumerical.title: Deriving Economic TPPC from Balance Sheet Funded Status
given: Beginning Net Funded Status = -120M USD (Underfunded: Assets 480M USD, PBO 600M USD)
Ending Net Funded Status = -155M USD (Underfunded: Assets 510M USD, PBO 665M USD)
Employer Cash Contributions paid to Plan = 40M USD
steps: Step 1 (Change in Funded Status) = Ending Funded Status - Beginning Funded Status = -155M - (-120M) = -35M USD.
Step 2 (Economic TPPC) = Employer Contributions - ΔFunded Status = 40M - (-35M) = 40M + 35M = 75M USD.
Step 3 (Interpretation) = The pension deficit widened by 35M USD despite paying 40M USD in cash, creating a true 75M USD economic cost.

definition: A measure of the sensitivity of a bond's price to benchmark yield curve parallel shifts, taking into account how future cash flows change as interest rates shift (mandatory for bonds with embedded options such as callables, putables, and MBS).
practicalUses: Accurately measures interest rate risk for callable bonds where modified duration fails due to negative convexity.
Immunizes institutional liability streams against non-linear rate movements.
Essential for evaluating structured credit and mortgage-backed securities where prepayments accelerate when rates drop.
commonPitfalls: Applying Modified Duration instead of Effective Duration to bonds with embedded options.
Forgetting the factor of 2 in the denominator (represents the double-sided rate shift: +Δy and -Δy).
Using nominal yields rather than benchmark par curve shifts (ΔCurve).

workedNumerical.title: Effective Duration of an 8-Year Callable Corporate Bond
given: Price if benchmark curve shifts down 30 bps (PV-) = 103.20
Price if benchmark curve shifts up 30 bps (PV+) = 99.40

definition: The second-order Taylor series approximation combining modified duration (first derivative) and convexity (second derivative) to accurately estimate a bond's percentage price change for large yield movements.
practicalUses: Eliminates large estimation errors when yields change by 100+ basis points.
Quantifies the positive asymmetry of straight bonds (prices rise more when rates fall than they drop when rates rise).
Evaluates barbell vs bullet portfolio performance under yield curve volatility shifts.
commonPitfalls: Forgetting the 1/2 factor in the convexity term: 0.5 × Convexity × (Δy)^2.
Squaring percentage basis points incorrectly: e.g. 150 bps must be entered as 0.0150, so (0.0150)^2 = 0.000225.
Omitting the negative sign on the duration term.

workedNumerical.title: Bond Price Response to a 150 bps Yield Surge
workedNumerical.result: Estimated Price Change = -10.22% | New Price = 879.87 USD

definition: Measures a bond or portfolio's price sensitivity to a shift in a specific segment or maturity of the benchmark yield curve (e.g. 2Y, 5Y, 10Y, 30Y) while holding all other key benchmark rates constant.
practicalUses: Decomposes portfolio exposure into steepener, flattener, and butterfly curve movements.
Reveals hidden curve reshaping risk in duration-matched barbell vs bullet structures.
Guides interest rate swap overlays to immunize specific cash outflow maturities.
commonPitfalls: Assuming that matching aggregate effective duration protects against yield curve shape changes (twist/butterfly).
Forgetting that the sum of all key rate durations equals the portfolio's effective duration for parallel shifts.
Overlooking that callable bonds have negative key rate durations at certain maturities near the call date.

workedNumerical.title: Portfolio Value Impact from Yield Curve Steepening
given: Curve Steepening Shift: 2Y falls by 40 bps (-0.0040), 5Y unchanged (0), 10Y rises 25 bps (+0.0025), 30Y rises 60 bps (+0.0060)

definition: The interest rate for a future period implied by current zero-coupon spot rates under the no-arbitrage principle, equalizing the return of rolling over short-term investments vs locking in a long-term rate.
formula: (1 + z_B)^B = (1 + z_A)^A \times (1 + f_{A, B-A})^{B-A} \implies f_{A, B-A} = \left[ \frac{(1 + z_B)^B}{(1 + z_A)^A} \right]^{\frac{1}{B-A}} - 1
practicalUses: Pricer benchmark for Forward Rate Agreements (FRAs), interest rate swaps, and futures.
Evaluates whether riding the yield curve or locking in a forward contract yields excess return.
Enables investors to compare market expectations against their proprietary rate forecasts.
commonPitfalls: Confusing notation: 2y1y means a 1-year rate beginning 2 years from today (A = 2, B = 3).
Arithmetic approximation error: using (B×z_B - A×z_A) / (B - A) without geometric compounding.
Failing to annualize rates correctly when dealing with semiannual coupon yield conventions.

workedNumerical.title: Computing the 1-Year Forward Rate Starting 2 Years from Today (2y1y)

definition: The constant spread added to the benchmark spot yield curve across all nodes of an interest rate tree that equates the theoretical backward-inducted price of a bond to its observed market price after explicitly removing the value of embedded options.
formula: \text{OAS} = \text{Z-spread} - \text{Option Value (in bps for Call)} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{OAS} = \text{Z-spread} + \text{Option Value (for Put)}
practicalUses: Allows direct credit and liquidity comparison between callable bonds and option-free straight bonds.
Identifies cheap vs rich bonds: if Market OAS > Fair Credit Spread, the bond is undervalued.
Determines whether the issuer or investor is being adequately compensated for volatility risk.
commonPitfalls: For a callable bond: OAS < Z-spread because the investor sold an option to the issuer (the option has positive cost to the investor).
For a putable bond: OAS > Z-spread because the investor bought an option from the issuer.
Assuming OAS is constant across different interest rate volatility assumptions (higher assumed volatility reduces OAS for callables).

workedNumerical.title: Extracting Embedded Call Option Value from OAS and Z-Spread
given: Option-Adjusted Spread (OAS from calibrated binomial tree) = 135 bps
steps: Step 1 (Relationship for Callable) = Z-spread = OAS + Option Value.
Step 2 (Option Cost in Spread bps) = Z-spread - OAS = 185 bps - 135 bps = 50 bps.
Step 3 (Economic Interpretation) = The investor is giving up 50 bps of annual credit spread to the issuer as payment for the call option.
workedNumerical.result: Embedded Call Option Value = 50 bps (Z-spread = 185 bps, OAS = 135 bps)

regexPattern: \b(Credit Default Swap Upfront|CDS Upfront Premium|CDS Upfront)\b
definition: The cash amount exchanged at inception of a standardized Credit Default Swap contract to bridge the difference between the standardized fixed coupon (100 bps for investment grade, 500 bps for high yield) and the fair market credit spread.
practicalUses: Calculates the exact cash settlement required to enter or unwind a standardized CDS position.
Enables liquid trading and clearing without non-standard customized coupons.
Measures rapid credit quality deterioration or recovery in real-time.
commonPitfalls: Sign convention: If Credit Spread > Fixed Coupon, the Protection BUYER pays the upfront premium to the seller.
If Credit Spread < Fixed Coupon, the Protection SELLER pays the upfront premium to the buyer.
Forgetting that spread duration (SDUR) is used, not modified duration of reference bonds.

workedNumerical.title: CDS Upfront Payment on High-Yield Issuer Downgrade
steps: Step 4 (Direction) = Since Market Spread (680 bps) > Fixed Coupon (500 bps), Protection BUYER pays 1,530,000 USD upfront.

definition: The monetary value of expected credit losses on a counterparty derivative or risky bond over its life, equal to the difference between the risk-free price of the instrument and its default-risky price.
practicalUses: Pricer adjustment for counterparty credit risk on OTC swaps, forwards, and complex derivatives.
Mandated under Basel III regulatory capital charges for commercial and investment banks.
Identifies underpriced risky assets when expected loss is greater than observed credit spreads.
commonPitfalls: Confusing Marginal Probability of Default (PD in specific period t given survival to t-1) with Cumulative PD.
Forgetting the discount factor (DF_t) when summing expected losses across multiple future payment dates.
Confusing Loss Given Default (LGD = 1 - Recovery Rate) with Recovery Rate.

workedNumerical.title: Two-Period CVA for a Corporate Bond
given: Year 1: Exposure = 1,040 USD; Marginal PD = 1.50%; Discount Factor (DF1) = 0.9615
Year 2: Exposure = 1,000 USD; Marginal PD = 2.00%; Discount Factor (DF2) = 0.9246

definition: The difference between a bond's Macaulay duration and the investor's intended investment horizon (Macaulay Duration - Investment Horizon). It dictates whether an investor is net exposed to price risk or reinvestment risk.
practicalUses: Determines immunization status: when Duration Gap = 0, price risk and reinvestment risk perfectly offset for a one-time parallel rate shift.
If Duration Gap > 0, investor is net exposed to PRICE RISK (rising rates hurt total return).
If Duration Gap < 0, investor is net exposed to REINVESTMENT RISK (falling rates hurt total return).
commonPitfalls: Using Modified Duration instead of Macaulay Duration in the horizon gap formula.
Assuming Duration Gap = 0 immunizes against non-parallel twists or steepeners in the yield curve.
Forgetting to rebalance over time: as time elapses, Macaulay duration decreases at a different rate than the horizon.

workedNumerical.title: Immunization Analysis for a 7-Year Horizon Portfolio
given: Market Interest Rates surge by 150 bps immediately after purchase
steps: Step 2 (Risk Exposure Identification) = Since Duration Gap > 0, the portfolio is dominated by PRICE RISK.
Step 3 (Impact of Rate Rise) = The capital loss from selling the bond at Year 7 exceeds the extra reinvestment income from higher coupon compounding; realized return < initial YTM.
workedNumerical.result: Duration Gap = +2.20 years (Net Price Risk Dominant)

regexPattern: \b(Free Cash Flow to Equity|FCFE|Levered Free Cash Flow)\b
definition: The cash flow generated by a firm's operations that remains available for distribution to common shareholders after fulfilling all operating expenses, net interest expenses, tax obligations, and reinvestment requirements in working capital and fixed capital, and adjusting for net borrowing.
practicalUses: Direct valuation model for levered common equity using the Cost of Equity (r) as the discount rate.
Ideal for companies whose dividend payouts diverge drastically from internal cash generation capacity.
Evaluates whether current dividends and share repurchases are sustainable without eroding liquidity.
commonPitfalls: Discounting FCFE using WACC instead of the Cost of Equity (r_e).
Forgetting to add Net Borrowing (Debt Issued - Debt Repaid) when deriving from Net Income.
When target debt-to-asset ratio (DR) is constant: FCFE = NI - (1 - DR) × (FCInv - Depr) - (1 - DR) × WCInv.

workedNumerical.title: Deriving FCFE from Net Income with Target Debt Ratio
given: Target Debt Ratio (DR) maintained = 40% of net capital investments
steps: Step 1 (Net Capital Expenditures) = FCInv - Depr = 55M - 25M = 30M USD.
Step 4 (FCFE Calculation) = Net Income - Equity Reinvestment = 80M - 24M = 56M USD.

definition: A fundamental dividend discount model that values equity assuming dividends grow at a constant perpetual rate (g). It also allows decomposing equity share price into the no-growth earnings value (E1 / r) and the Present Value of Growth Opportunities (PVGO).
practicalUses: Valuation baseline for mature, cash-cow dividend-paying companies (utilities, consumer staples).
Determines implied cost of equity or implied sustainable growth rate from market prices.
Decomposes stock price to quantify how much of current market capitalization reflects speculative growth vs established earnings power.
commonPitfalls: Using D0 (dividend just paid) in the numerator instead of D1 (expected next dividend = D0 × (1 + g)).
Violating the condition r > g: if growth rate exceeds the cost of equity, the model mathematically blows up.
Assuming sustainable growth (g = b × ROE) can exceed long-term nominal GDP growth in perpetuity.

workedNumerical.title: Valuation and PVGO Decomposition for Consumer Staple
given: Expected Next Year Earnings Per Share (E1) = 4.00 USD/share
steps: Step 1 (Expected Dividend D1) = D0 × (1 + g) = 2.40 × 1.05 = 2.52 USD/share.
Step 2 (GGM Intrinsic Value P0) = D1 / (r - g) = 2.52 / (0.09 - 0.05) = 2.52 / 0.04 = 63.00 USD/share.
Step 3 (No-Growth Value of Firm) = E1 / r = 4.00 / 0.09 = 44.44 USD/share.
Step 4 (PVGO Extraction) = P0 - (E1 / r) = 63.00 - 44.44 = 18.56 USD/share (29.5% of value).

definition: An equity valuation method that defines intrinsic value as the sum of current book value and the present value of all expected future residual income (net income minus an equity charge for the cost of capital).
formula: V_0 = B_0 + \sum_{t=1}^T \frac{\text{RI}_t}{(1 + r)^t} + \frac{\text{RI}_{T+1}}{(1 + r - \omega)(1 + r)^T} \quad \text{where} \quad \text{RI}_t = \text{NI}_t - (r \times B_{t-1})
practicalUses: Ideal for companies that do not pay dividends or have unpredictable/negative free cash flows.
Mitigates sensitivity to terminal value: typically 60-80% of total value is anchored by current book value on day zero.
Aligns valuation with economic value added (EVA) and competitive advantage decay (persistence factor ω).
commonPitfalls: Violation of Clean Surplus Relationship (CSR): Ending BV must equal Beginning BV + Net Income - Dividends (excluding OCI bypasses).
Confusing the persistence factor ω (0 ≤ ω ≤ 1): ω = 1 means perpetual constant RI; ω = 0 means RI vanishes immediately after forecast period.
Calculating the equity charge using ending book value rather than beginning book value (B_{t-1}).

workedNumerical.title: Single-Stage Residual Income Valuation with Persistence Factor
given: Current Book Value per share (B0) = 35.00 USD
Year 1 Residual Income persists into perpetuity decaying with ω = 0.60
steps: Step 1 (Year 1 Equity Charge) = r × B0 = 0.10 × 35.00 = 3.50 USD.
Step 2 (Year 1 Residual Income RI1) = Net Income - Equity Charge = 5.25 - 3.50 = 1.75 USD.
Step 3 (PV of Continuing RI with Decay) = RI1 / (1 + r - ω) = 1.75 / (1 + 0.10 - 0.60) = 1.75 / 0.50 = 3.50 USD.
Step 4 (Total Intrinsic Value V0) = B0 + PV of RI = 35.00 + 3.50 = 38.50 USD.

definition: The theoretically justified price-to-earnings multiple derived directly from fundamental drivers (dividend payout ratio, cost of equity, and sustainable growth rate) under the Gordon Growth Model.
practicalUses: Screens for market mispricing: if Actual Market P/E < Justified P/E, the stock is undervalued.
Isolates the sensitivity of valuation multiples to changes in corporate retention ratio (b) and ROE.
Provides an objective cross-check against peer average multiples.
commonPitfalls: Mixing up forward and trailing multiples: Trailing P0/E0 has the extra (1 + g) factor in the numerator.
Assuming higher dividend payout (1 - b) automatically raises P/E (if ROE > r, increasing retention raises P/E).
Failing to compute sustainable growth as g = b × ROE.

workedNumerical.title: Computing Justified Forward and Trailing P/E Ratios
steps: Step 1 (Sustainable Growth Rate g) = b × ROE = 0.60 × 15.0% = 9.0% (0.09).
Step 4 (Justified Trailing P/E) = (1 - b)(1 + g) / (r - g) = 0.40 × 1.09 / 0.02 = 21.8x.
workedNumerical.result: Justified Forward P/E = 20.0x | Justified Trailing P/E = 21.8x

definition: A capital-structure-neutral valuation multiple comparing the total market value of the operating enterprise (equity plus net debt plus preferred stock plus minority interest) to its pre-interest, pre-tax cash earnings (EBITDA).
formula: \text{EV} = \text{Market Cap} + \text{Total Debt} + \text{Pref Equity} + \text{Minority Interest} - \text{Cash and Equivalents} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{Multiple} = \frac{\text{EV}}{\text{EBITDA}}
practicalUses: Compares companies with vastly different debt leverage or tax jurisdictions without distortions.
Primary valuation metric in cross-border M&A transactions and Private Equity buyout (LBO) underwriting.
Useful for capital-intensive companies where depreciation policies diverge.
commonPitfalls: Failing to subtract Cash and Cash Equivalents when moving from Total Debt to Net Debt.
Comparing EV (an enterprise metric) to Net Income (an equity-only metric)—a severe mismatch.
Ignoring operating lease liabilities or underfunded pension deficits in Enterprise Value.

workedNumerical.title: Calculating Implied Equity Share Price from Peer EV/EBITDA Multiple
given: Total Debt on Balance Sheet = 350M USD
steps: Step 1 (Implied Enterprise Value) = EBITDA × Peer Multiple = 120M × 8.5 = 1,020M USD.
Step 2 (Net Debt) = Total Debt - Cash = 350M - 80M = 270M USD.
Step 3 (Implied Equity Value) = EV - Net Debt = 1,020M - 270M = 750M USD.
Step 4 (Implied Share Price) = 750M USD / 25M shares = 30.00 USD/share.

definition: The overall required rate of return for a company, calculated as the weighted average of the after-tax costs of each component of capital (debt, preferred stock, and common equity) weighted by their market values.
formula: \text{WACC} = w_d r_d (1 - t) + w_p r_p + w_e r_e = \left(\frac{D}{V}\right) r_d (1 - t) + \left(\frac{P}{V}\right) r_p + \left(\frac{E}{V}\right) r_e
practicalUses: Discount rate for Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF) enterprise valuation models.
Corporate hurdle rate for capital budgeting decisions (Net Present Value projects).
Economic profit benchmark: Economic Value Added (EVA) = Capital Invested × (ROIC - WACC).
commonPitfalls: Using book value weights instead of market value weights for debt and equity.
Applying the tax shield (1 - t) to the cost of equity or preferred stock (tax shield applies ONLY to debt interest).
Using historical coupon rates instead of the current marginal yield to maturity (YTM) for the pretax cost of debt.

workedNumerical.title: Corporate WACC Calculation with Target Market Weights
given: Market Value of Debt (D) = 300M USD (Current YTM rd = 6.0%)
Market Value of Equity (E) = 700M USD (Cost of Equity re = 11.5%)
steps: Step 3 (After-tax Cost of Debt) = rd × (1 - t) = 6.0% × (1 - 0.25) = 4.50%.

definition: A two-stage dividend discount model designed for firms whose high initial growth rate is expected to decline linearly over a transition period (2H years) until reaching a sustainable long-term perpetual growth rate (g_L).
formula: P_0 = \frac{D_0(1 + g_L)}{r - g_L} + \frac{D_0 \times H \times (g_S - g_L)}{r - g_L}
practicalUses: More realistic than abrupt two-stage models where growth drops instantly from 20% to 4%.
Values growth companies transitioning into mature market leaders as competitive advantages erode.
Decomposes value into normal terminal growth plus extraordinary transition excess returns.
commonPitfalls: Misinterpreting H: H is the HALF-LIFE of the transition period (if transition lasts 10 years, H = 5).
Using D1 instead of D0 in the excess growth term: the formula specifically requires base dividend D0.
Setting g_S < g_L: the H-model assumes a declining growth path (g_S > g_L).

workedNumerical.title: Valuing a Tech Leader with an 8-Year Growth Transition
steps: Step 2 (Base Terminal Value Component) = D0 × (1 + g_L) / (r - g_L) = 2.00 × 1.04 / 0.05 = 2.08 / 0.05 = 41.60 USD.

definition: A methodology to estimate the project or equity beta of a non-public or multi-division company by observing the equity beta of a publicly traded comparable firm, stripping out the peer's debt leverage (unlevering to asset beta), and reapplying the subject firm's target capital structure (relevering).
practicalUses: Estimates cost of equity for private equity buyouts and venture-backed private enterprises.
Derives divisional hurdle rates for diversified conglomerates (e.g. retail vs financial services arms).
Ensures equity risk measurement separates operational business risk from financial leverage risk.
commonPitfalls: Using D/V (Debt to Total Capital) instead of D/E (Debt to Equity) in the Hamada denominator.
Applying the subject firm's tax rate when unlevering the peer firm (must use the peer's tax rate to unlever and the subject's tax rate to relever).
Assuming debt has positive beta (standard CFA curriculum assumes risk-free debt, beta_debt = 0).

workedNumerical.title: Deriving Equity Beta for a Levered Private Health Division
given: Peer D/E Ratio = 0.50; Peer Tax Rate = 30%
Subject Project Target D/E Ratio = 0.80; Subject Tax Rate = 25%
steps: Step 2 (Asset Beta Interpretation) = Pure operational business risk of healthcare assets is 0.963.

definition: Risk-adjusted performance measures. The Sharpe Ratio penalizes both upside and downside volatility equally using total standard deviation, whereas the Sortino Ratio penalizes only returns falling below a user-specified Minimum Acceptable Return (MAR) using downside semi-deviation.
practicalUses: Evaluates hedge funds and options strategies with asymmetric, non-normal, or fat-tailed returns.
Sortino prevents managers with positive upside skewness (large winning outliers) from being penalized as 'risky'.
Universal benchmark for asset allocator mandate selection.
commonPitfalls: Sharpe Ratio assumes normally distributed returns (penalizes upside call option gains as risk).
In Sortino denominator, only deviations below MAR are included, but divided by total observations N or N-1.
Comparing Sharpe ratios across different time horizons without annualizing (multiply monthly Sharpe by sqrt(12)).

workedNumerical.title: Sharpe vs Sortino Comparison for Asymmetric Macro Fund
steps: Step 3 (Evaluation) = The high Sortino (1.25) vs moderate Sharpe (0.61) reveals the manager's volatility is predominantly desirable upside variance.

definition: Measures active return per unit of active risk (Tracking Error). Under Grinold's Fundamental Law of Active Management, IR equals Information Coefficient (IC) multiplied by the square root of Breadth (BR), scaled by Transfer Coefficient (TC) when constraints exist.
practicalUses: Evaluates active manager skill independent of broad market beta movements.
Enables investors to determine optimal active risk budgets using the expanded Sharpe formula: SR_p^2 = SR_b^2 + IR^2.
Directly shows how portfolio constraints (long-only rules, turnover limits) degrade alpha via TC < 1.0.
commonPitfalls: Confusing Information Coefficient (IC = correlation of forecasted vs realized return) with Transfer Coefficient (TC = correlation of forecasted active weights vs actual active weights).
Assuming Breadth equals total universe count (Breadth equals the number of INDEPENDENT forecast decisions made per year).
Comparing unconstrained vs constrained managers without adjusting for TC.

workedNumerical.title: Fundamental Law Expected IR and Sharpe Expansion
given: Transfer Coefficient (TC due to long-only constraint) = 0.75
steps: Step 2 (Expected Information Ratio) = TC × IC × sqrt(BR) = 0.75 × 0.08 × 12 = 0.7200.
Step 3 (Sharpe Expansion) = SR_max = sqrt(SR_b^2 + IR^2) = sqrt(0.50^2 + 0.72^2) = sqrt(0.25 + 0.5184) = sqrt(0.7684) = 0.8766.

definition: Complementary risk-adjusted performance measures. The Treynor Ratio measures excess return per unit of systematic risk (Beta), whereas M-Squared (M²) re-levers or delevers the portfolio with the risk-free asset until its volatility matches the market index, expressing risk-adjusted performance in percentage points.
practicalUses: Treynor is the appropriate metric when evaluating a sub-portfolio that will be added to a fully diversified parent fund.
M-Squared translates abstract Sharpe ratios into tangible basis-point alpha understandable by trustees and clients.
Identifies whether apparent market outperformance is merely the result of borrowing leverage.
commonPitfalls: Using Treynor for an undiversified stand-alone fund (Treynor completely ignores unsystematic firm-specific risk).
Confusing the order of terms in M-squared: a positive M² indicates the manager beat the market after volatility equalization.
Failing to use beta for Treynor while using total standard deviation for Sharpe.

workedNumerical.title: Calculating Treynor and M² for an Equity Fund
given: Portfolio Return (Rp) = 15.0%; Portfolio Beta = 1.25; Portfolio Volatility (σp) = 20.0%
workedNumerical.result: Treynor Ratio = 9.60% | M² = +1.00% (+100 bps vs Market)

definition: The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) specifies expected return based strictly on non-diversifiable systematic risk (Beta). Jensen's Alpha (α) is the excess return generated by the manager above the CAPM hurdle rate on the Security Market Line.
formula: E(R_p) = R_f + \beta_p [E(R_m) - R_f] \quad \text{and} \quad \alpha_p = R_{p, \text{actual}} - \left[ R_f + \beta_p (R_m - R_f) \right]
practicalUses: Primary hurdle benchmark for active fund performance attribution.
Evaluates whether a stock picker creates genuine structural alpha or merely holds high-beta market leverage.
Key cost of equity model in corporate finance and DCF valuation.
commonPitfalls: Using nominal equity risk premium instead of multiplying by beta: ERP = E(Rm) - Rf.
Assuming a high nominal return equals positive alpha (if Beta = 1.8 in a bull market, expected return is high and alpha may be negative).
Overlooking single-factor limitations: CAPM assumes market beta explains 100% of systematic return.

workedNumerical.title: Jensen's Alpha Attribution for a High-Beta Tech Fund
steps: Step 1 (Market Equity Risk Premium) = Rm - Rf = 12.0% - 3.5% = 8.5%.
Step 2 (CAPM Required Hurdle Rate) = Rf + Beta × (Rm - Rf) = 3.5% + 1.40 × 8.5% = 3.5% + 11.90% = 15.40%.
Step 3 (Jensen's Alpha) = Realized Return - Required Return = 17.50% - 15.40% = +2.10% (+210 bps).

definition: The mathematical formula for the variance of a portfolio combining two risky assets. It proves that whenever correlation (ρ) is less than +1.0, portfolio risk is strictly less than the weighted average risk of the component assets.
formula: \sigma_p^2 = w_1^2 \sigma_1^2 + w_2^2 \sigma_2^2 + 2 w_1 w_2 \text{Cov}_{1,2} = w_1^2 \sigma_1^2 + w_2^2 \sigma_2^2 + 2 w_1 w_2 \sigma_1 \sigma_2 \rho_{1,2}
practicalUses: Constructs the Markowitz efficient frontier of optimal risky assets.
Quantifies the 'free lunch' of diversification across uncorrelated asset classes (equities, commodities, bonds).
Determines the minimum-variance portfolio asset weights.
commonPitfalls: Forgetting the square root when converting portfolio variance (σp^2) to standard deviation (σp).
Missing the factor of 2 in the covariance cross-product: 2 × w1 × w2 × Cov(1,2).
Assuming that correlation (ρ) remains constant during market crises (correlations tend to spike toward +1.0 during liquidity shocks).

workedNumerical.title: Quantifying the Diversification Benefit of Equities and Treasuries
given: Correlation coefficient between Stocks and Bonds (ρ) = +0.10
steps: Step 6 (Weighted Average Volatility with no diversification) = 0.60(20%) + 0.40(8%) = 15.20% (Diversification bonus = -2.47% vol).

definition: A quantitative downside risk measure estimating the minimum dollar loss (or percentage loss) expected over a specified time horizon at a given probability level (e.g. 5% probability or 95% confidence) assuming a normal distribution.
practicalUses: Regulatory bank capital adequacy compliance (Basel III market risk capital).
Establishes institutional trading desk stop-loss limits and risk budgets.
Enables unified risk comparison across equities, fixed income, and currencies.
commonPitfalls: Normal distribution assumption fails during financial panics (ignores fat tails / excess kurtosis and negative skewness).
VaR does NOT state the maximum possible loss: it states the minimum loss suffered on the worst α% of days.
Scaling 1-day VaR to T-day VaR using sqrt(T) assumes returns are independently and identically distributed (no autocorrelation).

workedNumerical.title: Calculating 1-Day 95% Parametric Dollar VaR
steps: Step 3 (Interpretation) = There is a 5% probability that the portfolio loses at least 193,400 USD on any single trading day.

definition: A metric measuring the proportion of a fund's portfolio holdings that differs from its benchmark index. It ranges from 0% (pure index replica) to 100% (zero overlapping positions with benchmark).
practicalUses: Identifies 'closet indexers' (funds with Active Share < 60% charging high active management fees for index returns).
Used alongside Tracking Error to classify manager style: High Active Share + Low Tracking Error = Diversified Stock Picker; High Active Share + High Tracking Error = Concentrated Active.
Empirical indicator of fund alpha potential after fees.
commonPitfalls: Forgetting the factor of 1/2 in the formula (since absolute positive deviations must equal absolute negative deviations).
Assuming high Active Share guarantees outperformance (it guarantees deviation from benchmark, but stock selection can be poor).
Confusing Active Share (asset holdings difference) with Tracking Error (standard deviation of return differences).

definition: A linear asset pricing framework that models the expected return of an asset as a linear function of multiple macroeconomic or fundamental risk factors, each with its own factor beta and factor risk premium.
practicalUses: Decomposes portfolio risk into explicit macroeconomic drivers (GDP growth, unexpected inflation, credit spread changes).
Used by institutional factor models (MSCI Barra, Axioma) for risk attribution and factor tilt hedging.
Identifies pure arbitrage opportunities when assets with identical factor betas trade at different expected returns.
commonPitfalls: Using realized factor return instead of factor surprise (unexpected shock = Actual - Expected).
Confusing macroeconomic factor models (factors are surprises) with fundamental factor models (factors are standardized attributes like P/E, size).
APT does not theoretically identify what the factors are (unlike CAPM, factors must be empirically discovered).

workedNumerical.title: Calculating Expected Return Under a 2-Factor APT Model
given: Factor 1 (GDP Growth Surprise): Factor Beta β1 = 1.20, Factor Risk Premium λ1 = 4.0%
Factor 2 (Inflation Surprise): Factor Beta β2 = -0.50, Factor Risk Premium λ2 = 2.0%
steps: Step 1 (GDP Factor Premium Contribution) = β1 × λ1 = 1.20 × 4.0% = +4.80%.
Step 2 (Inflation Factor Premium Contribution) = β2 × λ2 = (-0.50) × 2.0% = -1.00%.
